vignette:
Kwame was eight years old when his father, a man he trusted to keep him safe, beat him with a leather belt until the buckle left a crescent-shaped bruise on his thigh. The abuse had happened many times before, but that night was the worst—his father’s rage erupted because Kwame had spilled milk across the kitchen floor. Decades later, the memory did not come as a coherent story. When Kwame tried to deliberately recall what happened, he found only fragments: the metallic snap of the belt buckle, his mother’s muffled weeping from the other room, the sudden weight of his father’s hand on his shoulder. These pieces never fit together, and yet when they surfaced they felt more real and vivid than anything else in his day—the way the linoleum felt cold against his cheek, the smell of his father’s sweat, the terrible stillness afterward. An old photograph of his father, unearthed while sorting through his mother’s belongings, would trigger a sudden, disjointed flash of that night, the memory dissolving before Kwame could grasp it whole.

Now twenty-two and a middle-school principal in a busy suburban district, Kwame carried a quiet conviction that he had permanently changed for the worse. This conviction worked like a magnet: the more he believed himself irreparably broken, the more often the disjointed memory fragments surfaced, as though his mind were determined to prove him right. That belief was reinforced every time a fragmented image flooded back. The vividness of these memories—more real than ordinary recollections—only deepened his certainty that he was irreparably broken, that the boy who had been beaten had become someone else entirely. He also lived with a gnawing fear that he could not stop bad things from happening to him or to the children in his care. That fear reshaped his perception of the school day, so that minor disruptions like a sudden fire drill or a child’s unexpected tantrum now stood out as triggers—events that had once been routine became charged with the power to throw him back into the memory of his father’s rage. This helplessness made him hyper-alert to any hint of unpredictability: a sudden fire drill, a child’s unexpected tantrum in the hallway, a parent showing up unannounced. Each unpredictable situation activated his terror that he would lose control of his own anger and do something terrible, just as his father had done. When chaos erupted in the school—a fistfight between eighth graders, a last-minute schedule change—Kwame felt his jaw clench and his pulse race, his mind flashing to the belt buckle, the sting, his own smallness.

In turn, the fragmented memory itself, when it intruded, left him so disoriented that he had learned to brace himself for the aftermath. On nights when he woke from a nightmare, the images clung to him, and the dream residue—the echo of his father’s voice, the ache in his thigh—became a fresh trigger, pulling him back into the unreachable shards of the past. His belief that he had changed for the worse made him avoid deliberately thinking about the abuse altogether, which paradoxically made his deliberate recall even more patchy and effortful. Over the months, Kwame began to micromanage his school day with rigid schedules, trying to eliminate all unpredictability. He stopped eating lunch in the faculty lounge because the open-ended chatter felt threatening. When his girlfriend, Amina, suggested they look through old family photos for a holiday card, he made an excuse and left the room. She noticed he never seemed to relax, that he flinched at sudden noises in their apartment. Their conversations grew stilted; he could not explain why he felt so constantly on edge.

Last week, Amina found him sitting on the bathroom floor at three in the morning, still shaken from a nightmare. She pleaded with him to see a therapist. That morning, Kwame agreed, not because he believed he could change, but because he was terrified that his anger—the rage he felt coiled beneath his skin whenever a third-grader defied him—would one day break free. He feared he was already becoming the man he most loathed. What he hoped for, more than anything, was to prove that he was not permanently damaged—that the fragments of his past could stay where they belonged.
